answers_by_date.basis: Constitution art. 19 No. 10 inciso quinto (1980 wording, before Ley 19.876): basic education is compulsory and the State must finance a free system to ensure access 'de toda la poblacion'. The CRC (in force since 1990) supported this. Both reach every child on the territory whatever their status, but no instruction specific to migrants existed yet. The only practice evidence is a later academic account: access problems for migrant children, seen by Mineduc in the 1990s, were 'still evident' in the early 2000s. It covers irregular children chiefly, and evidence for this period is thin.

The same constitutional guarantee, rewritten by Ley 19.876 (in force 22-05-2003) to cover basic and secondary education for 'toda la poblacion'. The Migrant Workers Convention (Decreto 84, art. 30) entered into force for Chile only in mid-2005, and Mineduc Ord. 07/1008 (1531) came only in August 2005, so neither counts on this date. Practice: the CRC's 2007 concluding observations found migrant and refugee children still discriminated against, 'particularly in their reduced access to education'.

Constitution art. 19 No. 10, plus CMW art. 30 (Decreto 84/2005: school access may not be denied because of irregular status) and Ley 20.370 (LGE, published 12-09-2009). The LGE's art. 4 says 'La educacion es un derecho de todas las personas' and requires a free compulsory system for the whole population. Mineduc Ord. 07/1008 (2005) allowed provisional enrolment whatever the migration status. Practice: the CMW Committee (2011) welcomed the Ord. but found that in some cases irregular children got no diploma, had their grades left out of the national register, or were refused re-enrolment.

Same legal base as 2010; the LGE was refunded into DFL 2/2009 with the guarantee unchanged. Practice: irregular children were generally admitted under provisional enrolment. But pupils on a 'RUT 100' provisional number were 'estudiantes fantasma', not registered in SIGE and cut off from benefits until Ord. 894/2016 and the IPE (January 2017). The CRC (2015) noted enduring discriminatory practices against immigrant children.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

events.instrument: Ley 19.876, Reforma constitucional que establece la obligatoriedad y gratuidad de la educacion media
events.what_changed: Replaced the inciso that made basic education compulsory and free for the whole population, extending it to secondary education. Coverage of 'toda la poblacion' was kept, so the indicator's answer is unchanged.
events.passage: Sustituyese el inciso quinto del numeral 10o del articulo 19 de la Constitucion Politica de la Republica, por el siguiente: La educacion basica y la educacion media son obligatorias, debiendo el Estado financiar un sistema gratuito con tal objeto, destinado a asegurar el acceso a ellas de toda la poblacion.

events.instrument: Decreto 84 de 2005, Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores
events.what_changed: Promulgated the Migrant Workers Convention, which entered into force for Chile 1 July 2005. Art. 30 expressly bars denying or limiting school access because of a parent's or the child's irregular status. This adds an explicit treaty basis for irregular children.
events.passage: El acceso de los hijos de trabajadores migratorios a las instituciones de ensenanza preescolar o las escuelas publicas no podra denegarse ni limitarse a causa de la situacion irregular en lo que respecta a la permanencia o al empleo de cualquiera de los padres, ni del caracter irregular de la permanencia del hijo en el Estado de empleo.

events.what_changed: An administrative instruction, not law, creating provisional enrolment for migrant pupils whatever their or their parents' migration status. Known only from a secondary source (the original was not read).
events.passage: en agosto de 2005 el Oficio ordinario 07/1008-1531 apunto a asegurar el ingreso, la permanencia y el ejercicio de los derechos de los alumnos inmigrantes en los establecimientos educacionales, con independencia del estatus migratorio del menor y de sus padres. Para tal efecto creo la figura de la matricula provisoria

events.what_changed: Replaced the LOCE's general provisions. It states education is a right of all persons and that the State finances a free compulsory system for the whole population, with principles of universality, integration and interculturality. The coverage stays the same.
events.passage: Articulo 4o.- La educacion es un derecho de todas las personas. ... La educacion basica y la educacion media son obligatorias, debiendo el Estado financiar un sistema gratuito destinado a asegurar el acceso a ellas de toda la poblacion

events.what_changed: Updated Ord. 07/1008 and introduced the IPE (from January 2017), which replaced 'RUT 100' so that pupils without a RUN, whatever their status, are registered and can receive benefits. This is administrative practice; the originals were not read.
events.passage: el Ordinario 329/2017 (que complementa el ordinario 894/2016) y que establecio la entrega por parte del Ministerio de Educacion del Identificador Provisorio Escolar (IPE), un numero unico que se entrega a todos los estudiantes que no contaban con un numero de identificacion nacional definitivo (RUT), independiente a su estatus migratorio.

answers.sourcing_note: LeyChile did not render the body of the Constitution. The 2003 change is dated from the text of Ley 19.876, and the pre-2003 wording is reconstructed from it. The LGE 2009 version and Decreto 84 were read directly. The Mineduc ordinarios (2005, 2016, 2017) were not read in the original, only through academic sources and the CMW Committee. A reported 2003 Interior Ministry circular could not be found. Practice evidence for 2000 is thin and indirect.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation rests on Ley 21.325 art. 17, which was not in force on 1 January 2020 (in force February 2022). The 2020 answer must rest on Constitution art. 19 No. 10, LGE art. 4, CMW art. 30 and the Mineduc ordinarios; the protection answer still holds on that basis. The implementation rating 'Effectively Always' looks high for 2020. The sources document persistent gaps: the RUT 100 'ghost students', fixed only by the IPE in 2017; the CMW 2011 findings on diplomas and re-enrolment; and continuing problems reported around 2019-2020. 'Usually' would fit the evidence better.
answers.notes: No court ruling was relied on. Treaties (CRC; CMW via Decreto 84/2005) are relied on as ratified human-rights treaties binding state organs under Constitution art. 5 inciso 2. Part of the 2000 Yes rests on the constitutional text 'toda la poblacion', which is a specific free-education guarantee rather than a general equality clause. The Mineduc ordinarios are administrative instructions and are treated as practice evidence, not law.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: No statute specific to migrants. Higher and adult education were reached by Constitution art. 19 No. 10 and the ratified ICESCR art. 13. Regular residents could enter public institutions on the same fee-paying terms as nationals. Study required a student visa or residence under DL 1.094, and irregular migrants lacked the ID needed to enrol. There is no practice evidence for this period; the rating is inferred.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Same as 2000. CMW art. 43(1)(a),(c) gives documented migrant workers equal access to educational and vocational-training institutions, subject to admission requirements. It entered into force for Chile only in mid-2005, after this date. No practice evidence on adult or higher education was found for this period.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: CMW art. 43 now in force for regular migrant workers. Ley 20.370 (LGE, 12-09-2009) art. 3(a) says education must be within reach of all persons throughout life. Access for irregular migrants still depended on ID and visa. Practice: the CMW Committee (2011) found irregular children sometimes denied diplomas and grade registration, which blocks progression to higher studies. No direct evidence on adult education was found.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, but only for certain visa types and migrant statuses (e.g., economic, family, humanitarian, temporary or regular migrants)
answers_by_date.basis: Same legal base as 2010. Free tuition (gratuidad) did not yet exist in statute: it began in 2016 through budget-law glosas and was put into statute by Ley 21.091 in 2018. Practice: academic sources report that migrants without a definitive RUN still had problems registering for the university entrance test. Regular residents generally accessed institutions.

answers.sourcing_note: Ley 21.091 arts. 1 and 103 were read in their current text; the publication date is from LeyChile. The LOCE, the DL 1.094 student-visa articles, the gratuidad budget glosas of 2016-2017 and the beca and loan rules could not be read. The pre-2018 answers are therefore inferred from the constitutional and treaty base and from general knowledge of admission practice.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation includes Ley 21.325 art. 17, which was not in force on 1 January 2020; the 2020 answer rests on Ley 21.091 arts. 1 and 103 alone. The citation also says 'permanent residents', but art. 103 reaches temporary residents too if they completed secondary school in Chile.
answers.notes: No court ruling was relied on. The CMW (Decreto 84/2005) is treated as binding under Constitution art. 5 inciso 2. The pre-2018 partial answer rests on constitutional and treaty provisions plus visa-based admission, with little direct sourcing. Practice evidence on adult and vocational education (EPJA, SENCE) for migrants was not found for any period.
